cards.front: When markup is based on selling price, what is the base (100%)?
back: [[imp:Selling price (SP) is the base.]]
Cost and markup are parts of the selling price.
Example: SP = $23, markup = $5 → markup is 21.74% of SP.
$$\text{Percent Markup on SP} = \frac{\text{Dollar Markup}}{\text{Selling Price}} \times 100$$
The denominator is always selling price, not cost.
cards.front: How do you calculate percent markup on selling price?
What is the formula for selling price when cost and percent markup on SP are known?

Example: Cost \$30, 40% on SP → S = 30 ÷ 0.60 = \$50.

cards.front: How do you find cost when selling price and percent markup on SP are known?
back: $$C = S \times (1 - r)$$
Cost is the complement of the markup rate times SP.

cards.front: Why is percent markup on selling price always smaller than percent markup on cost for the same item?
back: [[imp:Selling price is larger than cost.]]
Dividing the same dollar markup by a larger base (SP) gives a smaller percent.
Example: Markup \$5, cost \$18 → 27.78% on cost; SP \$23 → 21.74% on SP.

cards.front: How do you convert a percent markup on cost to a percent markup on selling price?
back: $$\text{\% on SP} = \frac{\text{\% on Cost}}{1 + \text{\% on Cost}}$$
Use decimal forms. Example: 40% on cost → 0.40 ÷ 1.40 ≈ 0.2857 = 28.57% on SP.
[[imp:Always divide by (1 + cost-based rate).]]
$$\text{\% on Cost} = \frac{\text{\% on SP}}{1 - \text{\% on SP}}$$
Use decimal forms. Example: 20% on SP → 0.20 ÷ 0.80 = 0.25 = 25% on cost.
[[imp:The percent on cost will always be larger.]]

cards.front: If a store buys a jacket for \$18 and wants a 21.74% markup on selling price, what is the selling price?
What is the complement of the markup rate when markup is on selling price?
back: [[imp:Complement = 1 − r (decimal)], where $r$ is the percent markup on SP.]]
The complement tells what fraction of the selling price is cost.
Example: r=25% → complement=0.75 → cost is 75% of SP.
[[imp:Multiply selling price by the complement.]]
cards.front: A retailer says the markup is 30% on selling price. If a TV sells for \$500, what did the store pay?
What is the blueprint aid for solving markup problems when the markup is on selling price?
back: Same three steps: Understand → Solve → Conclude.
1. Identify knowns: cost, selling price, or markup rate (and type).
2. Choose the correct formula: $S = C/(1-r)$ or $C = S(1-r)$.
3. Verify using $S = C + M$.
[[imp:Markup on cost:]] $S = C \times (1 + r)$, $C = S \div (1 + r)$.
[[imp:Markup on SP:]] $S = C \div (1 - r)$, $C = S \times (1 - r)$.
Never mix the two; always check which is the base.
